proposals.relationship: Bederman explicitly credits Foucault’s discourse analysis with shaping her study of knowledge, material practice and power, while stressing contradiction and possible agency.
proposals.evidence_note: Own methodological declaration at printed24, followed by three specified uses of discourse analysis on24–25. Note97 identifies The History of Sexuality, vol.1 and Power/Knowledge; note29 also includes the former. No exclusive genealogy, agreement with every Foucauldian position or independent reading of Foucault’s originals. Note97 prints an unverified1972 date for Power/Knowledge; this is not silently adopted as an edition fact.

proposals.relationship: Bederman includes Butler’s Gender Trouble among the theoretical resources for treating gender as a historical process connecting bodies, identities and authority.
proposals.evidence_note: Body7 develops an ideological-process account; note29 directs readers first to Teresa de Lauretis and then, among plural resources, to Butler1990, Foucault1978, Denise Riley1988 and Scott1988/1992. A bounded, explicitly cited conceptual resource; not a claim of personal mentoring, sole derivation or full adoption. Original Gender Trouble unread.

proposals.relationship: Bederman includes Scott’s gender-history and experience writings among the theoretical resources for her historical account of gender and authority.
proposals.evidence_note: Body7/n29 names Gender and the Politics of History (1988) and Experience in Feminists Theorize the Political (1992), edited jointly by Judith Butler and Scott,22–40. De Lauretis, Butler, Foucault and Riley retain co-credit. This is use of a particular theoretical bibliography, not proof that Bederman adopted all Scott’s arguments; cited originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Bederman credits Higginbotham’s analysis of race and gender among recent theoretical discussions informing the intersection she investigates.
proposals.evidence_note: At5 Bederman explicitly adopts Hazel Carby’s call to interrogate racial specificity and whiteness. Note23 also identifies Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, together with Berger/Brown/Hewitt and Lerner, as important recent theoretical discussions. This plural, bounded historiographic resource does not replace the more direct Carby credit or imply exclusive derivation. Higginbotham original unread; no guessed correction of the date as printed in Bederman’s note.

proposals.relationship: Bederman draws on Ryan’s Cradle of the Middle Class to connect early middle-class formation, manly self-restraint and gendered family practices.
proposals.evidence_note: Body11–12 with notes38–40/43–44 explicitly supports these historical explanations. Davidoff and Hall’s joint Family Fortunes is credited alongside Ryan; Blumin, Paul E. Johnson and Cott supply other aspects. No independent collation of Ryan1981 or wholesale adoption of her account.

proposals.relationship: Bederman uses Davidoff and Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes for the place of manliness and gendered family practices in middle-class formation.
proposals.evidence_note: Note38 expressly judges some observations from the English study applicable to the United States; body11–12 and notes40/42–43 use that joint work alongside Ryan, Cott and others. Both coauthors retain equal credit. This is a qualified transatlantic resource, not an assertion that English and American class formation were identical. Family Fortunes (1987) unread independently.

proposals.relationship: Bederman uses Cott’s histories of womanhood and feminism in explaining gendered middle-class identity and challenges to established male authority.
proposals.evidence_note: Body11/n40 cites The Bonds of Womanhood (1977) alongside Ryan and jointly authored Davidoff/Hall;14/n53 cites The Grounding of Modern Feminism (1987) with Mari Jo Buhle and Filene. Note96 also points to Cott’s Two Beards (1990) as another discussion of civilization, without making that a personal formative claim. Cott originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Bederman uses Higham’s accounts of nativism and cultural reorientation as resources for connecting white middle-class manhood to immigrant politics and the appeal of boxing.
proposals.evidence_note: Body13/n50 links immigrant contests for city government to power and manhood, citing Strangers in the Land (1971 consulted edition) with Gossett. Body17/n72 cites Reorientation,78–79 for boxing’s wider middle-class attraction. This scoped use coexists with her criticism of a masculinity-crisis formulation; it is not evidence of complete agreement. Originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Bederman qualifies the masculinity-crisis interpretation represented in part by Higham, arguing that ongoing change and contradictory authority claims do not by themselves establish a crisis of male identity or power.
proposals.evidence_note: Body10–11 acknowledges merit in both crisis and domesticity interpretations, then distinguishes remaking gender from evidence that men lost confidence in male identity and authority. Note36 names Higham’s Reorientation alongside Dubbert, Filene, Kimmel and McGovern; note37 credits Marsh and Griffen’s corrective. A bounded collective criticism, not rejection of all Higham’s work; her separate uses of his nativism and boxing discussions remain.
primary_locators: Manliness and Civilization (1995),10–11/notes36–37 (printed243), with15 reiterating remaking rather than crisis.

proposals.relationship: Bederman uses Roediger’s Wages of Whiteness in explaining how white working men linked manly independence to exclusion of Black men.
proposals.evidence_note: Body20/n84 supports the specific contrast between white male claims to independence and exclusions shared by women and Black men. The note identifies Roediger1991; nearby Berthoff and Horton/Horton discussions have distinct claims. No independent reading of Wages of Whiteness or inference of personal affiliation.

proposals.relationship: Bederman cites Lears’s account of neurasthenia among the resources for explaining anxieties about allegedly depleted white middle-class male vitality.
proposals.evidence_note: Body14/n54 uses No Place of Grace (1981),49–57 with Gosling, the jointly authored Haller study, Rotundo and Lutz, alongside contemporary George Beard. This is a specific plural resource, not an exclusive origin for the book’s argument or an endorsement of the historical disease categories. The Lears original remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Bederman includes Hofstadter’s Social Darwinism in American Thought among the historiographic resources for her account of Darwinism’s American reception and its tensions with Protestant millennial expectations.
proposals.evidence_note: Body26 describes educated Americans understanding Darwinism through conflict and survival without the older providential telos. Note102 directs readers to Hofstadter’s1955 edition alongside Robert C. Bannister1979 and Cynthia Eagle Russett1976 for Darwinism’s reception in the United States. This is a particular plural historical resource, not personal formation or wholesale adoption of Hofstadter’s interpretation. Originals unread. The separate self-employment statistic at12/n45 carries no additional interpretive claim.
